content:
Christians hold that Paul's gospel came from Jesus himself, after his ascension. Paul says so in plain words: "For neither did I receive it from man, nor was I taught it, but it came to me through revelation of Jesus Christ" (Galatians 1:12).[1] The claim is the foundation of his authority, and his letters fill much of the New Testament.

The same letters show him receiving traditions from other believers, consulting the apostles in Jerusalem, and preaching a gospel whose centre differs from the gospel Jesus preached in Mark. Each of these bears on the claim.

This article aims to provide context to Paul's claim, insha'Allah, in five questions drawn from his own letters, set beside the Quran's account of what Jesus was given. The Quran names it: "We sent him the Gospel: therein was guidance and light, and confirmation of the Law that had come before him" (5:46).[2]

Paul wrote Galatians against teachers who told his Gentile converts to be circumcised and keep the Law, and who questioned his standing. His defence is that his gospel "is not according to man" and came by revelation (Galatians 1:11 to 12). God, he says, "called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the Gentiles" (Galatians 1:15 to 16).[1]

Galatians proves that Paul made the claim. It cannot prove that the revelation came from God, and history has no method for testing that. Muslims do not reject Paul because his claim is supernatural; the Quran is revelation. The question is whether what he said was revealed agrees with the revelation God gave Jesus.

To the Corinthians Paul writes: "For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day" (1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4).[1] Received and delivered are the words of a tradition handed on.

Michael Winger studied the tension between the two letters. He argues that for Paul tradition is "a human mechanism": the gospel is carried in human words but made known "only by divine power", and the apparent contradiction "results from the different arguments he makes in the two letters".[3] On his reading, Paul learned formulas from others and held that their meaning was revealed to him. Either way, Paul's teaching drew on what others had handed him, and the claim that nothing came "from man" needs that qualification.

Three years after his conversion Paul went up to Jerusalem "to visit Peter, and stayed with him fifteen days", and saw James, "the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:18 to 19). Fourteen years later he went again and laid his gospel before the leaders "privately before those who were respected, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain" (Galatians 2:2).[1]

He reports that James, Cephas and John gave him "the right hand of fellowship" for a mission to the Gentiles (Galatians 2:9). He reports, in the same chapter, that he opposed Peter to his face at Antioch.[1] We set out that quarrel in Paul and Peter at Antioch. The record shows both contact and conflict, and it leaves his independence from the disciples his own claim.

In Mark, Jesus begins by "preaching the Good News of God's Kingdom, and saying, 'The time is fulfilled, and God's Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News'" (Mark 1:14 to 15). Asked for the greatest commandment, he answers: "Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one" (Mark 12:29).[1]

Paul's gospel has a different centre: "For I determined not to know anything among you, except Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2).[1] B. J. Oropeza's survey of a century of scholarship on Paul's gospel finds the debate turning on its origin, its content and his use of the word euangelion, whose sacred sense, he notes, is missing from the Jewish Scriptures.[4]

The Quran gives Jesus' message in his own words: "It is Allah Who is my Lord and your Lord; then worship Him. This is a Way that is straight" (3:51).[2] Apostle of Doom sets the two portraits side by side in two portraits of ʿĪsā.

Paul rests his standing on sight: "Haven't I seen Jesus Christ, our Lord?" (1 Corinthians 9:1).[1] Acts tells the vision three times and differently, and no one but Paul saw Jesus in it. We set out the three accounts in the Damascus road.

Christians weigh Paul by Scripture and the church's tradition. Muslims weigh every claim about Jesus by the revelation the Quran confirms, which gives the message of every prophet as one: "Not a messenger did We send before thee without this inspiration sent by Us to him: that there is no god but I; therefore worship and serve Me" (21:25).[2] A claimed revelation that makes Jesus divine fails that test. Whether Paul believed what he said is a separate question, and the record cannot answer it.

The bottom line

Paul claimed that his gospel came by revelation and not from man. His own letters show him receiving traditions, consulting Peter and James, and placing the cross at the centre where Jesus, in Mark, placed the kingdom of God and the oneness of God. Winger's reading reconciles the two letters by separating words from meaning, and leaves Paul's teaching drawn in part from others.

The Quran gives Jesus a Gospel of guidance and light, and gives his message in one line: "worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117).[2] The question is whether Paul's gospel is that message, and on the centre of it, the record and the Quran answer that it is not. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Galatians 1:11 to 19; 2:2; 2:9; 1 Corinthians 2:2; 9:1; 15:3 to 4; Mark 1:14 to 15; 12:29 (World English Bible).
  2. Quran 3:51; 5:46; 5:117; 21:25, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Michael Winger, "Tradition, Revelation and Gospel: A Study in Galatians", Journal for the Study of the New Testament 16, no. 53 (1994), pp. 65–86, doi:10.1177/0142064X9401605304.
  4. B. J. Oropeza, "The Gospel According to Paul: Over a Hundred Years of Interpretation", Religions 15, no. 12 (2024), article 1566, doi:10.3390/rel15121566.
